subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: East African sleeping sickness is a rapid, fatal disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense transmitted by the tsetse fly. Early recognition of fever, lymphadenopathy and neurological changes is essential for timely treatment.

sections.p: A zoonotic disease endemic to East Africa, it progresses quickly from fever to neurological involvement, often within weeks.
Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense is a protozoan with a slender, flagellated body and a variant surface glycoprotein coat that evades immunity.

t.b: Detects motile trypomastigotes; positive confirms infection
Screening test; positive supports diagnosis but cross‑reacts with other trypanosomes
Highly sensitive; confirms species and stage when available

sections.p: Tsetse flies ingest trypanosomes from infected animals; parasites develop in the fly and are transmitted during subsequent bites.

t.b: Identifies tsetse presence; informs vector control

sections.p: After a brief hemolymphatic phase, parasites cross the blood‑brain barrier, causing meningoencephalitis and characteristic sleep disturbances.
b: Stage 2: neurological signs, sleep cycle disruption

t.b: Elevated white cells >5/µL indicates CNS involvement

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with laboratory confirmation; staging guides therapy.

t.b: Positive supports diagnosis; negative does not exclude

sections.p: First‑line drugs are pentamidine for stage 1 and suramin for stage 2; supportive care and monitoring are critical.

t.b: Renal function for pentamidine; liver enzymes for suramin

sections.p: Remember the rapid progression of the rhodesiense form; early treatment with pentamidine prevents CNS invasion.

t.b: Malaria, typhoid, HIV encephalopathy; consider trypanosomiasis when fever is unresponsive to antimalarials

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid onset fever with lymphadenopathy, unexplained headache, confusion, or sleep cycle changes; any suspicion of tsetse exposure

faq.q: How long does it take to progress to neurological stage?

faq.a: Yes, with appropriate drug therapy started before CNS involvement.
No vaccine is available; prevention relies on vector control and early treatment.
